html:
The Napoleonic Code is the French Civil Code, put into force in 1804 under Napoleon. It set out in one clear book the law of persons, property, contracts and families, and was copied across Europe and far beyond.

Before the Revolution, France had hundreds of local legal systems, Roman law in the south and customary law in the north, plus church law for marriage. The Revolution promised a single code but never finished one. Napoleon, as First Consul, set up a commission of four jurists in 1800 and chaired many of its meetings himself.

What it said:

  • All male citizens are equal before the law; there are no birth privileges.
  • Property is protected and can be freely sold; feudal dues are gone.
  • Contracts freely made bind the parties.
  • Marriage is a civil act, and divorce was allowed, though on narrow terms.
  • The husband rules the household; a wife owes him obedience and needs his consent for most legal acts.

It drew on Roman law and older French custom, and it was written to be read by ordinary citizens. French armies took it into Belgium, the Netherlands, parts of Germany and Italy, and it stayed after they left. Later it shaped the civil codes of much of Latin America, Louisiana and Quebec, and influenced codes in the Middle East.

Much has been amended since, especially on the status of women, but it is still in force in France. Napoleon said in exile that his true glory was not his forty battles but his Civil Code.
sum: The Napoleonic Code is the French Civil Code, put into force in 1804 under Napoleon. It set out in one clear book the law of persons, property, contracts and families, and was copied across Europe and far beyond.
